lesson.title: Zooming In on the Leftovers: Building a Residual Plot
lesson.summary: A residual plot graphs each residual against its x-value, magnifying the leftover scatter so patterns invisible on the original scatterplot jump out.
lesson.body:
Once you have calculated a residual for every point in a data set, the natural next step is to graph them. A residual plot puts the explanatory variable x on the horizontal axis, just like the original scatterplot, but replaces y on the vertical axis with the residuals themselves. Every point in a residual plot answers the same question: at this x-value, how far did the model's prediction miss, and in which direction? Because the vertical axis now shows leftovers instead of raw scores, a residual plot acts like a magnifying glass, stretching out small deviations from the line that can be hard to see when they are squeezed against a steep trend in the original scatterplot.

Continue with the study-hours example: (1, 55), (2, 65), (3, 70), (4, 80), (5, 88), with fitted line y-hat = 47.3 + 8.1x. The five residuals calculated earlier were -0.4, 1.5, -1.6, 0.3, and 0.2, for x = 1 through 5 respectively. The residual plot has five points: (1, -0.4), (2, 1.5), (3, -1.6), (4, 0.3), (5, 0.2). Notice that a horizontal reference line is drawn at residual = 0; this line represents the regression line itself, since every point on the original line has a residual of exactly zero. Points above the reference line were underestimated by the model, and points below it were overestimated. The vertical scale of a residual plot is usually much smaller than the vertical scale of the original scatterplot, since residuals are only leftovers rather than full score values, and that compressed scale is precisely what makes small patterns easier to spot.

Drawing this plot by hand is straightforward once residuals are computed: mark x on the horizontal axis exactly as before, mark the residual value on the vertical axis, and plot the point. Software and graphing calculators do this automatically once a regression is run, which is one reason residual plots are used constantly in practice even though the underlying arithmetic is simple. Many statistics packages will even offer to plot residuals against the predicted values y-hat instead of against x directly; for a simple linear regression with one explanatory variable, the two versions show the identical pattern, just relabeled along the horizontal axis, so either one is a valid tool.

What makes the residual plot valuable is not the individual points but the overall shape they form. In the study-hours example, the residuals bounce between positive and negative with no obvious rise, fall, or curve, which is a first clue that a straight line is a reasonable model for this relationship. Compare that to a case where the true relationship is curved: for data following y = x-squared at x = 1 through 5 (y = 1, 4, 9, 16, 25), fitting a line gives residuals of 2, -1, -2, -1, 2. Plotted against x, those five points trace a clean U-shape, dipping down in the middle and rising at both ends.

That U-shape is the entire point of building the plot in the first place: it makes a pattern that was hidden in the original scatterplot (where the steep upward trend can mask curvature) impossible to miss. A scatterplot of the x-squared data still looks fairly smooth and continuous to the eye, and a student could easily be fooled into thinking a line fits reasonably well; only after subtracting off the line's prediction at every point does the leftover curvature become obvious. Once a residual plot is constructed, the next task is reading what its shape is telling you, which is exactly the subject of interpreting residuals.
